pr_body:
Superceded by #86180.

Resolves godotengine/godot-proposals#990.

**Multi windowing *won't* be implemented in this PR due to some incompatibilities with Wayland's and Godot windowing API which have to be sorted out. Trust me, I tried. Doing otherwise would just stall everything. I'm sorry.**

The aim of this PR is to eventually implement a fully working `DisplayServer` compatible with the [Wayland protocol](https://wayland.freedesktop.org/) on Godot 4.x, which had architectural changes that led to the closing of #27463.

## Status

It is currently **beta quality**. It's definitely usable and most features are implemented but there's still lots of testing to do. 

As there's a growing need of this backend due to poor XWayland compatibility, the main focus of this PR is polishing and documenting the current feature set as best as we can so that we can get this merged and stable by 4.3. Everything that's not implemented yet will be implemented post-merge.

For ease of testing this PR will track, whenever possible, the latest (pre)release closer to `master`.

Current version tracked: **4.2-stable**

For a list of what's missing and of known issues see below.

## Testing

Thanks to GitHub Actions, every commit is built and the result can be downloaded up to 90 days since the last change. See [Testing pull requests](https://docs.godotengine.org/en/stable/contributing/workflow/testing_pull_requests.html) for info on how to get a build.

**Note: for users without an account, the steps outlined in the documentation are broken. Instead of putting a link to the workflow file in nightly.link, go to checks, click on a random job on the left bar and copy/paste the URL up to `runs/NUMBERS`. You'll be able then to download the latest build.**

This means that usually there's no compilation required as it's already done for you.

At startup the engine will try initializing a Wayland display. If it fails, it prints an error and tries with X11. There's no need to have both libraries installed to run the executable as they're dynamically loaded at runtime if available.

Note that it's always possible to force the X11 backend to start first (triggering XWayland if available) by appending the `--display-driver x11` argument.

This PR is also completely HiDPI aware and includes fractional scaling (except for the cursor). Note that there are still some known issues with the HiDPI implementation in the cases of fractional scaling.

## Building

If for whatever reason there's the need of building this branch from scratch, a plain `scons` invocation should work fine, building an hybrid dynamically loaded X11/Wayland executable.

Every new header and dynamic library wrapper is embedded in the source, so there are no extra build dependencies to download, with the current exception of `wayland-scanner`, required for generating protocol wrappers at build time.

## Stuff not done yet

### Important methods missing
- `window_set_mouse_passthrough` (Wayland doesn't support polygonal regions, only rect regions). We could implement a bounding box approximation, but an entirely new rect-based API like https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/8568 would be better

### Big features missing
 **NOTE: Due to the urgency of this PR (and general eligibility), this list is purely informative and should not be treated as an hard roadmap for merging.**
 - Virtual keyboard
 - IME
 - Native file selection dialog
 - Touch input (I have to find/make some Linux-powered touch screen first)
 - Screen recording (screen_get_pixel and screen_get_image, requires Pipewire support)

### What about xdg-desktop-portal?

xdg-desktop-portal is essential for interacting with modern Wayland desktop environments but it should not be implemented in this PR directly. Luckily there is already a growing support for it upstream.

## Known issues

### This PR's

- We don't have a lot of support code for older/newer globals yet.

- Under certain unkown situations, when heavy work is done on the main thread, it's possible to block the Wayland thread and crash the engine due to a Wayland event queue overflow.

- The low processor usage time is always set to 500 µs (0.0005 ms) due to latency concerns with manual frame throttling. 

- The cursor doesn't handle fractional scaling yet.

- Autoscale returns a rounded-up size when using fractional scale as it comes from the perspecitve of the screen. A better window-centric API/workaround is needed.

- Tablet support has been commented out as I didn't have a chance to refactor it during the `WaylandThread` split.

- The particular combination of `x11=no wayland=yes opengl=yes openxr=yes` fails to build.

### Wayland specific (stuff that we can't fix directly or requires workarounds)

- It looks like libdecor has some issues toggling server-side decorations.

- I'm not really sure if we have a reliable way of setting size non-interactively. As such `DisplayServer::window_set_size` is currently a no-op. Further investigation is required.
 
- At least on sway, it looks like DnD doesn't update the cursor properly. I can replicate this outside Godot so this might be a compositor bug.

### Godot specific (stuff that looks related to this PR but is actually not)

- Scrolling on a touchpad is a little bit too fast. See #49873.

- The shaders' `TIME` variable is wrong when the window is "hidden" (which is most of the time for us due to Wayland reasons). A proposed fix and more info is available over at #82222.

- The splash doesn't resize. This means that tiling WMs will have a wrongly sized window until the end of loading. There's no clean way of improving this and, while hacks are definitely possible, I'm not sure that it's currently worth it.

## Thanks to

 - @ddevault and @toger5, from which I initially took the key mapping code.
 - @dos1 for helping me with many, long, headache inducing things.
 - @leandro-benedet-garcia for helping with DRI_PRIME detection and other tweaks.
 - @smohantty for some very small build fixes.
 - @stalkerg for general help, improvements and debugging.
 - @vmedea for a bunch of very useful fixes.

I'm always open to external contributions (especially as I've never worked on anything like this before) be it patches, testing, reviews, general technical help or even just moral support, they're all very appreciated!

After some thinking I'm pretty sure that I should properly handle multiple seats and that whatever worked before (if it even works anymore) worked by pure chance.

For the (understandably) unititiated, Wayland handles multiple input devices in one session through the concept of seats, comprising of an optional pointer, keyboard and touchscreen each. These seats are used by compositors like sway to effectively implement [collaborative multi pointer support](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=WO2L_ihO_rI) (you read that right).

I'm not sure on what behaviour to give it though, but I think that, in high level terms, it should revolve around the concept of a current seat: when the editor detects an interaction from a pointer, keyboard or (eventually) touch screen that is not the current one, it cleans up the current state (for example it unconstrains the pointer if applicable), looks for the seat from which this new pointer/keyboard came from, makes it the new current seat and sets its state like the previous one (like pointer constraint status etc), so that for whatever reason one might switch from one seat to the other cleanly and easily.

What do you guys think?

Ok this is a kinda hard announcement to write, but I fear that implementing (a fully working) subwindow support might not be worth it if not impossible, considering both the limitations of the Godot and Wayland API.

In short: Godot expects windows to be universally configurable, with arbitrary children, while Wayland separates window types and expects popups to be created and deleted in order, stacked on top of a toplevel.

Long version: The crashes that happened on sway(wlroots)/mutter are attributable to a (pretty important) detail that imposes popups to be deleted in order of creation, from the last created to the first. Apparently they're stacked relative to a toplevel, which means that a popup can't have more than one children and that operations in between the stack are extremely hard. Weston/Kwin worked fine due to implementation details but sway(wlroots)/mutter are right too.

Thus I assume that, without extensive changes in the Godot API to account for this behaviour (which I think that aren't either ideal nor doable in time for the release), subwindows, and more specifically popups, aren't implementable due to huge differences in the expected windowing model.

Now, if nobody has something else to say, the question becomes whether to remove most subwindow code, making the patch smaller and removing a lot of maintenance burden, or to patch it out just "temporarily" until we can finally implement this properly without rewriting a lot of code. I'm inclined to simplify as much as possible, but I'm interested in hearing other people's opinion.

Ok, I talked quite a while with some people regarding the whole "borderless window" thing, and currently the Godot DisplayServer API is simply not (reasonably) compatible with Wayland in that regard.

Subsurfaces are not made for borderless windows for a variety of reasons, and as such an implementation can crop/mess them as much as they want outside of the window. The argument that really convinced me is that delegating positioning to the compositor (like with `xdg_popup`s) is the only way to avoid borderless windows going outside of an output (since we can't know the absolute position of windows).

Still, while everything can still be put to discussion (like why xdg-popups are stacked instead of in a tree like fashion), talking with the people at #wayland@irc.ofct.net we concluded that, as is, it'd require quite a bit of work to implement a proper multiwindow Wayland backend for Godot.

For further reading, there's the sway discussion at https://github.com/swaywm/sway/issues/4924 and the IRC log: https://oftc.irclog.whitequark.org/wayland/2022-10-17

So, the plan for now is to force single-window mode, polish the few things left, put this up to review, merge this PR (hopefully before the 4.0 release) and then think on a nice way of making multiwindow support work with wayland in a cleaner way.

Time to talk about the new stuff I've been working on.

In short, I'm making an experiment to refactor most code and make it more maintainable as I've never felt really satisfied with it under that aspect.

I've based it on the HiDPI branch I had locally and improved that feature too, so if you want to test it, go to my `wayland-thread-refactor` branch over at https://github.com/Riteo/godot/tree/wayland-thread-refactor

For the technical people, please keep reading for a rationale and some notes. As usual, I also write some notes in my commits so that you can hopefully always keep track of whole thing if you want.

Edit: in the end I'm breaking lots of stuff right now lmao, input handling's really messy.

## The technical part

As soon as I came back from the sprint I started thinking on what would be the next steps to do and settled on two big, somehow related, things: HiDPI support and making the code more maintainable.

I say that they're related because at the sprint we decided to do the whole scaling manually, which in short requires us to keep track of _both_ the logical and scaled window sizes (naming might differ in code, I haven't still settled on it), which is a mess and requires to "translate" lots of position data backwards and forwards.

I never liked the code a lot because we passed a huge `WaylandState` struct between all objects and, while this approach allows a very fast iteration cycle, it binds everything together. I never used the API before this PR so that was definitely a great advantage but now that I have more experience I'm sure I can untangle the code a lot.

The HiDPI implementation was the nail in the coffin for me, so, based on the hacked in HiDPI branch I've begun a big refactoring stemming from two important observations:
 1. We can avoid most uses of the `WaylandState` struct by using Wayland object references in a more clever way: we can fetch directly and _anywhere_ (not only in the event handlers) the custom data  we assign to the objects (such as `WindowData` for `wl_surface`s). This will also avoid useless loops in which we looked for data with an associated object as we can do the opposite instantly and have the same result. We can also tag objects to make sure that we're actually working with Godot Wayland objects and make sure that the object's actually initialized correctly (a thing I had no idea was possible before working on HiDPI, thank libdecor for that).
 2. The Wayland event handlers do pretty much only a few things really, such as "async" stuff (e.g. instantly resizing the window wayland-side, responding to xdg-shell pings, attaching the cursor as per-spec), translating data (e.g. input events, scaled window data) and sending it to the main thread through our dedicated `InputEvent`-like event queue. In short, the interface leans heavily into being almost mono-directional, with most main-thread side stuff being simple Wayland-related requests through the native Wayland queue (_not_ our custom unrelated one). 

So, I've decided to give a shot to an approach I've always been skeptical about (and of which I still am to an extent): moving all Wayland stuff into a `WaylandThread` class. The main ways of interfacing with Wayland will be its own methods, so that we can move all the "translation" stuff into a nice place, and all the incoming data from the thread will be available through an event queue. The usage feels almost like the Vulkan driver with lots of low-level, yet Godot-aware, requests.

The idea is that `DisplayServerWayland` shouldn't care about _most_ Wayland technicalities (that's the point I'm a bit skeptical about, hence the "most") but instead only comb through the right data and do the right requests through `WaylandThread`, which will do all the annoying stuff.

Input handling is very messy too (I mean, this is a messy problem by nature) and I'm still not sure on how to fit it into the equation but I'm starting to become optimistic. I have some ideas though.

In theory we should also be able to move locking only into the Wayland-Godot event queue operations, which should theoretically reduce lock contention if that's even an issue. Not really a priority/goal of this refactoring but it would be a nice side effect.

Keep in mind that this is all an experiment and at the time of writing there are still a lot of transitional hacks to migrate the code slowly without breaking or rewriting everything from scratch in one go.

That said, I would really like to know your opinions on this experiment.

## In short

- Most of the Wayland-specific code and the polling thread got put into a class named (fittingly) `WaylandThread`, which handles most initialization, the message queue and scaling in a way that shouldn't hurt one's brain too much (especially due to scaling) while reading the whole thing.

- `WaylandState`, a "jack of all trades" struct got yeeted away in favor of getting the data associated with Wayland objects and `WaylandThread`'s methods, along other stuff described in the comment before.

- Luckily very little things are a dumb wrapper and the rest makes it 100% worth it, scale is handled automatically and _just works_.

## Extra notes

- Along the properties in the comment before, I've explicitly made `WaylandState` as less stateful as possible (outside of Wayland object handling of course). It still needs to have some state but the idea is that `DisplayServerWayland` will still have to keep track of stuff it touches, which avoids lots of issues and has actually improved stuff like cursor handling and the (hacky) pointer warping logic.

# All right, time for a new status update!

You might've noticed that this PR hasn't had updates in a while.

While I'm, as usual, doing other stuff, there's actually another big reason for my inactivity here: I've been doing some mad experiments lately (read: since the 5th of July) which sadly didn't really pan out as I hoped but taught me some cool stuff that's actually useful.

## First, the bad news
Yes, this was still a multiwindow attempt.

I'm aware at how much time this feature is sinking from me, but I genuinely don't like the idea of forcing single-window mode on users. I might have to live with it for now though.

Toplevels work fine, the problematic part is popup handling. In theory we could make floating editors and docks work fine, but since we have no clear API separation on what is a popup and what is not we have no practical way of adding special cases for either. Also, `WINDOW_FLAG_POPUP` doesn't count, as tooltips don't use it because they don't want input to be redirected to them. This makes that flag more of a `PopupMenu` flag than an actual "floating borderless window" flag.

I had an idea of tacking on windows a "class" enum, distinguishing them between `WINDOW_CLASS_TOPLEVEL`, `WINDOW_CLASS_POPUP` and `WINDOW_CLASS_POPUP_MENU` or something like that, but the almost-but-not-quite redundancy with `WINDOW_FLAG_POPUP` made everything ugly and the lines between the classes blurred too much for my taste.

This is a distinction that also X11 needs (tiling WMs beg for proper popup tagging), mind you, but finding a way that keeps compatibility and is not terribly redundant is hard. I really don't have the time nor the motivation to work on this as of now, plus this has to be discussed with the other platform maintainers, which is even harder, so this will have to be postponed once again.

The bad news don't end though: even if we changed all the APIs (I did some PoCs with the above idea), wlroots has a pretty nasty timing bug for us separate-event-thread users: https://gitlab.freedesktop.org/wlroots/wlroots/-/issues/3662

Luckily with some light testing it looks like KDE doesn't have it, but still, wlroots compositor users aren't few. Admittedly I've not talked about this with the wlroots people yet. There are some patches floating around which _should_ fix the problem but they're all WIP and so on.

I really want this to work one day though, I've not given up yet!

## (Finally) the good news

This was sort of planned. While I hoped that it would yield something usable, I knew this would've been a throwaway experiment, especially since I allowed myself to play with the core willy-nilly. It was a proof of concept after all.

I've not actually worked non-stop for more than a month. While I got a bit frustrated due to the asynchronous hard-to-debug nature of this sort of stuff and the compositor bugs, I've actually worked on this very sparsely. This was mostly due to personal factors such as tiredness unrelated to Godot.

Also, this resulted in some actually very useful code patches that I'll be applying soon™ here!

Since a main showstopper for multiwindowing was the ugly occlusion bug, I've actually found a really nice, pretty much "proper" workaround! It's a bit shoehorned in Godot's architecture and _might_ still give some weird problems, but it's our best bet I've not had any huge issues with it. I'm talking about handling the frame event manually, explained very clearly here: https://emersion.fr/blog/2018/wayland-rendering-loop/

(it's some annoying stuff so don't worry if you don't understand it right away)

Thanks to this fix, coming soon™, you'll be able to hide the window and have the game still tick!

Also there were issues with the event loop, since it could panic _before_ having the time to read (and print) the Wayland error message. Now most (all?) of the "Wayland error XX" messages should be accompanied with an actual textual reason on why the compositor disconnected us. Thanks to kennylevinsen over at #wayland at OFTC for pointing this out!

Another other thing I found out was, from what I can understand, that the actual thing closer to Godot's focus on Wayland is the keyboard focus, not the pointer focus like I thought. I haven't actually thoroughly investigated it but I recall talking about this on IRC. I think that makes more sense, so I'll probably bring that over here and see what happens.

Honestly, considering the stuff above and ignoring the big disappointment of not being able to pull this off even as a PoC, I'm actually very happy on the stuff I've learned, especially for the occlusion fix since now the usability improved considerably!

Note that the branch hasn't been uploaded online because it's a dumpsterfire of workarounds and attempts, with a metric ton of debug `print_line`s and failsafes attempting to figure out what's wrong with the complex asynchronous dance needed for multiwindowing.

I'll soon rebase this PR, fish out the good stuff and fix the few things that got broken by the refactoring.

Thanks for you patience!

@TuxTheAstronaut all right I've investigated further and it actually happens on both drivers. The fact that it works in the first place sometimes is just some blind timing luck.

The issue is kinda complex, so I'll try to simplify the issue as much as possible.

In short: due to the fact that Wayland tells us when we can draw, we have to treat (render-side) the window as almost always hidden.

That means that, just as when we don't have any visible window, the main loop goes faster.

The main loop is faster so we have a smaller delta time, which isn't really a problem, _but_ this smaller delta time is also passed to the shaders, which get called seldom since we're skipping drawing a lot. So the shader think that passed a lot less time than actually did since the last drawing.

The solution (I think) would be to pass to the shaders the actual time that passed since the last _actual_ draw.

@gerblesh hi!

Window positioning isn't the issue and instead something more intrinsic to the current Godot windowing API.

The issue is that there's no unambiguous way to know the class of the window we're going to create or, in other words, we have no sure way of knowing whether we're going to create an `xdg_toplevel` or an `xdg_popup`.

X11 actually has some similar issues since it has its own concept of a class (messing up stuff like tiling WMs) but its WMs are more lenient as it's pretty much tacked on, while on Wayland it's mandatory that we figure the right window type from the start, otherwise we get a really unusable mess (e.g. a tooltip registered as a toplevel would be catastrophic).

Fixing this, especially while preserving compatibility and not introducing duplicate or messy APIs would require _a lot_ of effort, and currently this PR as is is already a great improvement over the Wayland experience, especially for tiling compositor users like myself.

I'm really sorry that multi-windowing won't be implemented but I fear that a proper fix will require way more work outside of the Wayland backend itself.

That said, I want to note that, given the current constraints of the Wayland protocol, _it's more than doable_. We just have to figure out how to clear things up from our side, which I think will probably also make the life better for the users of other backends too in the long term.

issue_context.title: VisualShader node window closes when main window is in focus, breaks tiling WMs
issue_context.body:
### Godot version

v4.0.2.stable

### System information

Linux NixOS, using Sway as a tiling WM

### Issue description

When using the VisualShader system, if I try to add a node using either the "Add Node..." button or right-clicking on the graph, the new menu briefly appears as a new window but instantly closes when the main window is in focus.

This especially breaks on Linux tiling window managers such as Sway or i3 (when not using floating-layout) as the main window stays focused to prevent popups from forcibly grabbing focus.

Other types of windows, such as Editor Settings, do not have this issue as they stay open even if focus switches back to the main window.

I'd like to change this behavior to prevent the window from closing if the main window is in focus.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Open up any project that has a VisualShader resource.
2. Either click on "Add Node..." or right-click on the visual graph to make the node selector menu appear.
3. Bring your mouse back to the main window.
4. The node selector menu disappears without any other input.

### Minimal reproduction project

N/A
comments:
Okay, so while debugging this, I think I see two issues here:

1. On Linux, certain windows in Godot are not properly following the XDG shell protocol. Specifically, some popups in Godot are *not* properly being created as `xdg_popup`, but rather as a regular `xdg_surface`. This causes compositors to see them as their own root window and treat them differently. Some popup windows, such as the menu that appears when you right-click on text, *do* work properly.
2. Popup windows expect to close themselves if they are not in focus. This isn't really a bad behavior, but when combined with the first point, it causes the window to immediately disappear on systems that treat `xdg_surface` as their own window and *not* as a popup (in my case, Sway).
Enabling Single Window Mode in the Editor Settings allows me to use it properly. If anyone else runs into this issue, you can likely do the same.

> Enabling Single Window Mode in the Editor Settings allows me to use it properly. If anyone else runs into this issue, you can likely do the same.

Is there a way to reliably detect whether a tiling WM is being used (e.g. an environment variable or the presence of a file)? We could force single-window mode in this case, so that the user doesn't have to do it manually.

> Is there a way to reliably detect whether a tiling WM is being used (e.g. an environment variable or the presence of a file)? We could force single-window mode in this case, so that the user doesn't have to do it manually.

There's a couple of `$XDG_*` environment variables that you could use to determine this. For example, `XDG_CURRENT_DESKTOP` will be set to `i3` or `sway` on those environments. But that just tells you which environment you're in, there's not really any way to determine the *behavior* of the current desktop environment.

The best you'd be able to do is maintain a list of different environments and hardcode the default for each. But even that's difficult because some environments like GNOME and KDE have unofficial extensions that turn them into tiling WMs. I believe there's also some Windows and MacOS plugins for tiling functionality, and even some desktop environments made for VR (I have no idea how this behavior works on any of these).

The **safe** method would be to just use single-window mode as the default (or the default for Linux) until Wayland support is better fleshed out and window types more accurately follow the XDG Shell Protocol (or whatever the issue with Xorg is).
Can this also be replicated on i3? Otherwise I think it would be appropriate to put it in the XWayland issues tracker (yes there are enough issues to warrant one, the situation is that bad).
